newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO inflexible as violence continues.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO inflexible as violence continues.

text.p: A new cycle of Middle East violence enters its third week with Israel and the PLO showing few signs of flexibility.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday Israel would not resume peacemaking as long as Palestinian bombs kept exploding.
Arabs insist the starting point for renewed peace talks should be a halt to Israeli construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem which has touched off daily West Bank unrest.

All eyes turned to Middle East peace sponsor Washington to put forward a new peace initiative. U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he was "personally prepared to do anything I can" to put peace moves back on track.
A U.S. opinion survey published on Wednesday said Americans were blaming the Israelis and the Palestinians about evenly for the crisis.
"The peace process can't be conducted while buses or cafes are exploding or while children are in danger of a terrorist blowing them up," Netanyahu told reporters on Wednesday.

The Israeli leader spoke hours after a petrol bomb was thrown at an Israeli bus in the West Bank causing it to overturn and injuring 11 soldiers. It was the third bombing Israel blamed on Palestinians in two days.
In the West Bank north of Jerusalem on Wednesday, Israeli troops dispersed Palestinian stone-throwers with tear gas and rubber bullets.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called Palestinian President Yasser Arafat twice on Wednesday to hear his views ahead of a hastily arranged visit by Netanyahu to Washington next week.
Arafat told Albright the crisis stemmed from Israel's East Jerusalem settlement.
"The Israeli settlement policy... places the entire peace process in real danger," the official Palestinian news agency Wafa quoted Arafat as telling Albright.
Palestinians complain the settlement pre-empts the results of final peace talks yet to come on the status of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 and claimed by both sides.
Egypt, backing Arafat, called on Netanyahu to have the "courage" to back off the Jerusalem settlement.

"To save the peace process needs political statesmanship and courage. The practices and steps that have been taken in Jerusalem will have to be rolled back. This is the starting-point for any effort to save the process," Egypt's Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said in Cairo.

And Usama el-Baz, a senior political adviser to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, told journalists that the Middle East's nightmare -- the death of the peace process -- was possible if progress were interrupted for a long time.
"Consequences will be bleak for everybody," Baz said.
But Netanyahu said he would tell Clinton on Monday that halting the violence was the first priority.

"We will discuss the urgent need for the Palestinian Authority to start battling terrorism because without it we won't be able to move forward in the process," he said, adding that he did not expect U.S. pressure over his settlement policy.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington on Wednesday the United States would like Arafat to clamp down on militants "who are bent on violence and terror and who are using that as a political tactic."
In the PLO-ruled Gaza Strip on Tuesday, two Palestinians were killed in explosions that Israel said were botched suicide bombings by the Islamic Jihad group aimed at Jewish children.

Jihad sources said the Palestinian Authority had arrested 30 of their activists in overnight raids. But the group disavowed the two bombings, charging that Israel had staged them to divert attention from its settlement policy.
Foreign Minister David Levy vowed Israel would not order its bulldozers to stop work on the East Jerusalem neighbourhood.
"It is our right to build in Jerusalem. Period."
